entities.name: Church of San Juan of Portomarín
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Church of San Juan (or San Nicolás) of Portomarín in Galicia, northwestern Spain — one of the most architecturally unusual churches on the Camino de Santiago pilgrimage route — is a 12th-century Romanesque-Gothic church that was originally built by the Knights of Saint John of Jerusalem (Knights Hospitaller) and was relocated stone by stone to higher ground in 1962-1963 when the Portomarín valley was flooded to create the Belesar reservoir on the Miño River, making it one of the most dramatic modern examples of historic building relocation and one of the most remarkable architectural survivals on the entire Camino de Santiago.

Portomarín's original settlement in the Miño River valley was an important stage on the French Way (Camino Francés) to Santiago de Compostela — the most traveled pilgrimage route to the tomb of Saint James. The Knights Hospitaller church of San Juan was built in the 12th-13th centuries in the heavy defensive Romanesque style characteristic of military-religious orders. The church's fortress-like exterior (with battlements and few windows) was designed for both religious use and potential defensive purpose — reflecting the military order's dual nature.

The 1962 construction of the Belesar Dam requiring the valley's flooding created an unprecedented heritage challenge: the medieval village of Portomarín (and its remarkable church) faced permanent submersion. The Spanish government authorized the systematic relocation — stones were numbered, removed, transported up the hill, and reassembled at the new higher Portomarín. During droughts, the ruins of the original village occasionally re-emerge from the reservoir, creating an eerie visual reminder of the lost settlement. The relocated church continues to welcome Camino pilgrims.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Church of San Juan of Portomarín — a Knights Hospitaller Romanesque masterpiece, stone-by-stone relocated from a flooded valley in 1962, and one of the Camino de Santiago's most historically distinctive pilgrimage churches — combines medieval military-religious heritage with one of history's most remarkable modern building relocations.
